datasets.name: RLBench
datasets.eval_protocol: For the proposed few-shot challenge, split the 100 tasks into 90% meta-train and 10% meta-test tasks. At test time, provide K demonstrations of each unseen task and evaluate on new episodes/configurations; report 1-shot, 5-shot, and 20-shot results. The system must have no prior information about unseen tasks beyond the demonstrations. Report task success; each task gives a sparse +1 reward only on completion.

datasets.name: VLABench
datasets.eval_protocol: For fine-tuned VLAs, evaluate primitive tasks with seen and unseen object categories; also evaluate language-instruction generalization, unseen-but-similar tasks, and composite tasks. Primitive tasks are jointly trained on base and common-sense data within categories, with 100 trajectories sampled per task category (1,600 total); composite tasks are fine-tuned and evaluated separately within each task domain. Workflows use a single evaluation setting across ability dimensions. VLM evaluation uses a simulated-environment dataset: non-interactive evaluation matches generated skill-sequence graphs to references, while interactive evaluation measures task progress. The paper does not specify evaluation episode counts or splits for these evaluations.

baselines.name: OpenVLA
baselines.fair_comparison: Fine-tuned on the VLABench data using original code and default hyperparameters; the number of epochs was fixed for comparison across dataset sizes. OpenVLA used recommended LoRA, while Octo and RDT-1B were fully fine-tuned. Input views differed by model: OpenVLA and Octo use one view, RDT-1B uses three.

baselines.name: Octo
baselines.fair_comparison: Fine-tuned on the VLABench data using original code and default hyperparameters; the number of epochs was fixed for comparison across dataset sizes. OpenVLA used recommended LoRA, while Octo and RDT-1B were fully fine-tuned. Input views differed by model: OpenVLA and Octo use one view, RDT-1B uses three. Octo was trained for over five epochs because it was reluctant to converge.

baselines.name: RDT-1B
baselines.fair_comparison: Fine-tuned on the VLABench data using original code and default hyperparameters; the number of epochs was fixed for comparison across dataset sizes. metrics.name: Task success rate
metrics.caveat: The paper says the binary 0/1 success metric is better suited to straightforward skill learning; it introduces Progress Score for a more nuanced assessment.

metrics.name: Progress Score (PS)
metrics.caveat: The paper introduces PS as a graduated alternative to binary task success. It weights correct target decisions at 0.2 and completed task substeps at 0.8.

metrics.name: Skill Recall Rate (SR)
metrics.caveat: Described as the coarsest-grained skill-identification metric; reported alongside parameter recall, skill-parameter recall, and precise matching.

metrics.name: Skill&Parameter Recall Rate (SPR)
metrics.caveat: Requires correct skills and their exact associated parameters, and is described as stricter and more comprehensive than SR or PR; reported alongside them.

metrics.name: Precise Matching Rate (PM)
metrics.caveat: Evaluates skill-and-parameter matches while requiring logical dependencies, rather than imposing a totally strict sequence; reported alongside SR, PR, and SPR.

metrics.name: Weighted VLM total score
metrics.caveat: Combines SR, PR, SPR, and PM using predetermined weights that sum to 1; the component scores are also reported.

controls.name: Voxposer without visual perception
controls.detail: The text-only version receives ground-truth labels for object selection; it is compared with Voxposer using GPT-4V as the visual-perception module.
controls.rules_out: Helps distinguish performance with supplied object labels from performance when visual perception is added.

controls.name: VLA fine-tuned from scratch
controls.detail: Models trained from scratch on the fine-tuning dataset are compared with their pretrained counterparts on primitive tasks with seen objects.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the reported downstream performance is attributable to starting from pretrained models rather than training on the fine-tuning data alone.

controls.name: RDT-1B open-loop control
controls.detail: The main RDT setup uses open-loop inference with 64 trajectory points; the paper compares it with closed-loop control and also reports an open-loop 32-point setting.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether RDT’s low task performance is explained by open-loop error accumulation.

controls.name: VLM without chain-of-thought prompting
controls.detail: VLM performance with CoT prompting is compared with performance without CoT.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether performance differences are associated with adding CoT prompting.

controls.name: VLM few-shot settings with fewer examples
controls.detail: For Qwen2-VL, the paper compares few-shot settings from 0 to 7 examples.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether performance differences are associated with the number of few-shot examples.

controls.name: VLA training-data scales of 100, 500, 1,000, and 2,000 samples
controls.detail: The paper evaluates three VLA models on the same primitive-task setting at these dataset sizes.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether low performance is alleviated simply by increasing the amount of fine-tuning data.

confounds.name: RDT-1B’s low task performance is caused by open-loop error accumulation rather than model limitations
confounds.detail: Open-loop execution can accumulate errors, which could explain poor task completion without implying an inherent limitation of the model.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper evaluates RDT-1B with closed-loop control and reports only slightly better performance, concluding that low task success is primarily due to model limitations.

confounds.name: Low VLA performance is caused simply by too little fine-tuning data
confounds.detail: The low scores could reflect limited data quantity rather than difficulty adapting the models to the tasks.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper evaluates data scales of 100, 500, 1,000, and 2,000 samples; PS improves slightly, but task success remains low across scales.

evidence_standards.name: Repeated workflow evaluations aggregated into a final score
evidence_standards.detail: The paper says it evaluates each task several times and aggregates the scores, but does not state the number of repeats or report variance, confidence intervals, or statistical tests.

evidence_standards.name: VLM prompting setting used for reported comparisons
evidence_standards.detail: The VLM comparison is reported under 1-shot prompting, except GLM-4V-9B, which is evaluated 0-shot because it does not support multiple-image input.

datasets.name: D’Claw manipulation benchmarks (Pose, Turn, Screw)
datasets.eval_protocol: Figure 7 reports task success percentage for training on a physical D’Claw, measured with the task success evaluator over multiple runs; each timestep is 0.1 real-world seconds. The paper does not specify a split or number of evaluation runs.

datasets.name: D’Kitty locomotion benchmarks (Stand, Orient, Walk)
datasets.eval_protocol: Figure 7 reports task success percentage for training on a simulated D’Kitty, measured with the task success evaluator over multiple runs; each timestep is 0.1 real-world seconds. The paper does not specify a split or number of evaluation runs.

metrics.name: Dense reward
metrics.caveat: The paper says rewards are task-specific and can ignore real-world concerns such as safety, movement quality, hardware risks, and energy expenditure; it also provides sparse task score, success evaluation, and hardware-safety measures.

metrics.name: Sparse score
metrics.caveat: The paper presents score as a direct, unshaped task objective alongside dense reward; it does not state a specific caveat for the score.

metrics.name: Success percentage (success evaluator φ_se)
metrics.caveat: Success alone can conceal safety violations: the paper reports that policies can solve tasks while still exhibiting significant violations, and therefore reports safety violations alongside success.

metrics.name: Hardware safety violations (φ_hs)
metrics.caveat: The paper reports violations as counters over a finite horizon, including joint/position, velocity, and current/torque limits; it does not state a specific caveat for this measure.

datasets.name: WidowX Manipulation (Bridge setup)
datasets.eval_protocol: 48 trials per policy across two language-conditioned and two goal-conditioned tasks; over-the-shoulder camera view; actions sampled from the single-arm head.

datasets.name: Franka Manipulation (DROID setup)
datasets.eval_protocol: 39 trials per policy across two language-conditioned tasks; over-the-shoulder camera view; actions sampled from the single-arm head.

datasets.name: ALOHA Bimanual Manipulation
datasets.eval_protocol: 20 trials per policy across two language-conditioned tasks; uses overhead and two wrist camera views; actions sampled from the bimanual head.

datasets.name: LoCoBot Navigation
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on path-following, obstacle avoidance, and sharp corner-turning in 6 locations, with one trial per location and policy. A topological map of goals is collected; success is based on distance to the closest node in the map. Actions sampled from the navigation head.

datasets.name: Go1 Quadruped
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated for 25 minutes using proprioceptive observations and the quadruped action head; reports average reward normalized by the reward of the RL-trained expert policy that generated the data.

datasets.name: Tello Quadcopter
datasets.eval_protocol: Zero-shot evaluation in 3 locations, with one trial per location and policy. Uses the navigation head and maintains a static height while following its 2-D relative waypoints.

baselines.name: Single-robot dataset baseline
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper's policy architecture trained only on the target dataset for each evaluation setting. Because these datasets are smaller, the authors use smaller architecture versions (5M–95M parameters) to avoid overfitting.

baselines.name: Yang et al. [8]
baselines.fair_comparison: The authors directly use the 186M-parameter policy. For LoCoBot, both policies are trained on the same amount of LoCoBot data. For WidowX, Yang et al. use the same relevant Bridge data as CrossFormer plus additional WidowX data collected in their lab.

metrics.name: Average reward normalized by the RL-trained expert's reward

controls.name: Target-only single-robot training condition
controls.detail: Train the policy on only the target embodiment's dataset rather than co-training on data from multiple embodiments; smaller architecture versions are used for these smaller datasets to avoid overfitting.
controls.rules_out: A comparison against this condition tests whether the cross-embodiment-trained policy's performance can be accounted for by training on target-robot data alone.

confounds.name: Yang et al.'s low WidowX performance may result from a camera-view mismatch rather than the absence of manual alignment
confounds.detail: CrossFormer is evaluated using a third-person view. Yang et al. train with third-person and wrist views but input only one view at a time, which the authors hypothesize may cause underfitting to third-person control and could explain their zero success rate.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out by a reported measurement; the paper offers this as a hypothesis.

datasets.name: Robomimic
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates 5 tasks across 9 proficient-human/mixed-human variants, with both state- and image-based observations. Reports success rates averaged over the last 10 checkpoints across 3 training seeds and 50 environment initializations; also reports averages of best-performing checkpoints for consistency with the original evaluation.

datasets.name: Push-T (simulation; adapted from IBC)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates RGB observations and 9 ground-truth 2D keypoints with end-effector proprioception, under randomized initial conditions. Uses target-area coverage as the metric; reports averages over the last 10 checkpoints across 3 training seeds and 50 environment initializations, and also best-checkpoint averages.

datasets.name: Multimodal Block Pushing (BET benchmark)
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses scripted-oracle demonstrations that randomly choose which block and target to use first. Reports state-observation results as frequencies of pushing 1 or 2 blocks into targets (p1, p2); the general simulation protocol uses 3 training seeds and 50 environment initializations, averaging the last 10 checkpoints.

datasets.name: Franka Kitchen
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the dataset of 566 human demonstrations, each completing 4 tasks in arbitrary order. Reports state-observation frequencies of interacting with 1 or more through 4 or more objects (p1–p4); the general simulation protocol uses 3 training seeds and 50 environment initializations, averaging the last 10 checkpoints.

datasets.name: Real-world Push-T
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates the multi-stage task of pushing the T block into the target and then moving the end-effector to an end-zone. Commands are produced at 10 Hz and linearly interpolated to 125 Hz. IoU is measured at the final step; success is IoU above the minimum IoU in the human demonstrations. Reports IoU, success rate, and episode duration.

datasets.name: 6DoF Mug Flipping
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates 20 in-distribution initial conditions; success requires the mug lip to face down and the handle to point left.

datasets.name: 6DoF Sauce Pouring
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates pouring a ladle of sauce onto the center of the dough. Reports IoU between the poured-sauce mask and a nominal circle, plus success rate thresholded by minimum human performance.

datasets.name: Periodic Sauce Spreading
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates spreading sauce over pizza dough. Reports sauce coverage and success rate thresholded by minimum human performance.

baselines.name: LSTM-GMM (BC-RNN)
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper reproduces this method for simulation and reports its best-performing results. For real-world mug flipping, it is trained on a subset of the same data as Diffusion Policy. The paper does not state a generally matched hyperparameter-tuning protocol.

baselines.name: IBC
baselines.fair_comparison: Simulation results are taken from the original paper; no additional matched comparison protocol is stated. In real-world Push-T, IBC is evaluated with position- and velocity-control variants.

baselines.name: BET
baselines.fair_comparison: Simulation results are taken from the original paper; no additional matched comparison protocol is stated.

metrics.name: Success rate
metrics.caveat: For simulated Push-T, the paper uses target-area coverage instead. In real-world Push-T, success is defined by final-step IoU exceeding the minimum IoU in the human demonstrations; for sauce tasks, the threshold is minimum human performance.

metrics.name: IoU
metrics.caveat: For real-world Push-T it is measured at the final step rather than taking the maximum over all steps; the paper reports success rate and episode duration alongside it.

metrics.name: Episode duration
metrics.caveat: Reported alongside IoU and success rate for real-world Push-T.

metrics.name: Sauce coverage
metrics.caveat: Reported alongside success rate for periodic spreading.

metrics.name: p1, p2, p3, p4 task-completion frequencies
metrics.caveat: For Block Pushing, p1/p2 count episodes pushing 1/2 blocks into targets; for Kitchen, p1–p4 count episodes interacting with at least that many objects.

controls.name: Diffusion Policy with velocity control
controls.detail: The paper compares it with Diffusion Policy using position control.
controls.rules_out: A performance difference between these two Diffusion Policy conditions supports an effect of action-space choice, rather than attributing that difference to the diffusion policy being used at all.

controls.name: Diffusion Policy with shorter and longer action horizons
controls.detail: The paper varies the number of predicted actions executed before replanning and compares performance across horizons.
controls.rules_out: Shows whether the reported action-horizon choice, rather than simply using action-sequence prediction, accounts for performance and the responsiveness/consistency trade-off.

controls.name: Diffusion Policy with ImageNet-pretrained or R3M visual encoders
controls.detail: Compared with the end-to-end-trained visual encoder in real-world Push-T.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the reported visual-policy performance requires end-to-end encoder training rather than using the evaluated pretrained encoders.

confounds.name: Best-checkpoint reporting could inflate performance relative to typical training performance
confounds.detail: A best-performing checkpoint can make a method appear stronger than its usual evaluation performance, particularly when checkpoint performance is unstable.
confounds.ruled_out_by: For Robomimic and Push-T, the paper also reports averages over the last 10 checkpoints across 3 training seeds; it notes that best-checkpoint averages are included for consistency with the original papers.

confounds.name: The performance difference may be due to position control rather than the policy method
confounds.detail: Diffusion Policy is evaluated with position control while simulation baselines use velocity control, so action space could explain some of the headline comparison.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper separately compares Diffusion Policy with position and velocity control and discusses the action-space effect. This does not fully isolate method from action space in the cross-method simulation comparison.

confounds.name: Idle actions may contribute to baseline failures on real-world Push-T
confounds.detail: The paper says retaining idle actions contributed to LSTM-GMM and IBC tending to overfit to small actions and get stuck.
confounds.ruled_out_by: No separate measurement rules this explanation out; the authors state they retained idle actions because they are required for the task.

evidence_standards.name: Simulation evaluation
evidence_standards.detail: Reports averages over 3 training seeds and 50 environment initializations, using the average of the last 10 checkpoints. For Robomimic and Push-T, it also reports averages of best-performing checkpoints.

evidence_standards.name: Real-world trial counts
evidence_standards.detail: Reports 20 trials/evaluations for mug flipping; the Push-T discussion gives failures out of 20 evaluations, and the sauce-task discussion gives baseline failures out of 20 experiments.

evidence_standards.name: Real-world diffusion inference setting
evidence_standards.detail: Uses DDIM with 100 training iterations and 10 inference iterations; the paper reports 0.1-second inference latency on an Nvidia 3080 GPU.
