baselines.fair_comparison: Run on the same 10 task protocols, with the specified robot, scene, and 10 Hz control loop; 20 simulation repeats. Most settings were left at defaults.

baselines.name: V-Rep (Vortex)
baselines.fair_comparison: Run on the same 10 task protocols, with the specified robot, scene, and 10 Hz control loop; 20 simulation repeats. Most settings were left at defaults.

metrics.name: Euclidean distance error
metrics.caveat: The paper notes a small window of deviation in this and rotation error; pose error is also reported to better differentiate discrepancies in translation and/or rotation.

metrics.name: Inner product of unit quaternion error (rotation error)
metrics.caveat: The paper notes a small window of deviation in this and Euclidean error; pose error is also reported to better differentiate discrepancies in translation and/or rotation.

metrics.name: Pose error
metrics.caveat: Combines translation and rotation using a length scale chosen to weight them; the paper reports it alongside the separate Euclidean and rotation errors.

metrics.name: Velocity max, average and error
metrics.caveat: Dataset-to-simulation velocity error cannot be calculated for manipulable objects; the paper instead reports their maximum and average velocity over moving time.

metrics.name: Acceleration/deceleration max, average and error
metrics.caveat: The paper reports acceleration error over time for the arm, but uses maximum and average acceleration for manipulable objects.

metrics.name: Motor torque min, max and error
Contact force and contact moment max and error
Moving time
metrics.caveat: The paper uses this to characterize object movement; it highlights that rolling-time discrepancies can reveal when simulated contact does not occur.

metrics.name: Object translation and rotation distribution comparison (Mahalanobis distance)
metrics.caveat: Object trajectories are not directly comparable when their end poses differ. The paper instead compares final resting poses against multivariate normal distributions of the dataset’s final positions and Euler rotations, built from 20 trials.

evidence_standards.name: 20 repeats per task
evidence_standards.detail: The real-world task recordings and simulator evaluations use 20 repeats; the paper says the dataset repeats are intended to produce reliable measurements. It does not state a statistical test or a numerical threshold for deciding that two results differ.

datasets.name: Bridge
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated with Q1 and Q2 multiple-choice questions derived from demonstrations. Q1 selects a trajectory from four candidates; Q2 selects a picking point and then an ending tile. Public-dataset questions total 9,180 across Bridge and DROID: 6,120 Q1 and 3,060 Q2. Accuracy is averaged over questions; no split is stated.

datasets.name: DROID articulated
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated with Q1 and Q2 multiple-choice questions derived from demonstrations. Q1 selects a trajectory from four candidates; Q2 selects a picking point and then an ending tile. Public-dataset questions total 9,180 across Bridge and DROID: 6,120 Q1 and 3,060 Q2. Accuracy is averaged over questions; no split is stated.

datasets.name: DROID pick-and-place
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated with Q1 and Q2 multiple-choice questions derived from demonstrations. Q1 selects a trajectory from four candidates; Q2 selects a picking point and then an ending tile. Public-dataset questions total 9,180 across Bridge and DROID: 6,120 Q1 and 3,060 Q2. Accuracy is averaged over questions; no split is stated.

datasets.name: In-house fabric manipulation setup
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on 2,662 manually curated multiple-choice questions across ten dimensions. Questions have four choices; question augmentation is not used, and generally one question is formed per recorded scene. Data whose preprocessing failed is discarded. Accuracy is reported.

datasets.name: Simulation tasks (SimplerEnv, SoftGym, RLBench, and IsaacSim)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on Place Carrot, Close Drawer, Straighten Rope, Sweep Object, and Ball Shooting questions. Each question asks the model to choose among four candidate keypoints; simulation questions use ground-truth keypoints and no grid overlay. Accuracy is reported; no split or question count is stated.

datasets.name: Unseen real-world robot manipulation tasks
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on seven tasks using a UR5 arm, Robotiq 2F-85 gripper, and top-down RGBD camera. Models select keypoints from predefined options; success rate is reported, with three trials per task.

metrics.name: Multiple-choice accuracy
metrics.caveat: The authors note that MCQ evaluation depends on having preselected correct and incorrect options, unlike real-world settings where a model may need to generate actions directly. They also report real-world task success rates alongside benchmark accuracy.

metrics.name: Real-world task success rate
metrics.caveat: The authors note that the real-world experiments use the same predefined-option selection setup as the MCQs, so this does not establish performance when models generate actions directly.

metrics.name: Coefficient of variation across task categories
metrics.caveat: The paper uses lower CV to indicate greater robustness across categories; it also reports average accuracy, since a lower CV can accompany lower average performance.

metrics.name: Pearson correlation
metrics.caveat: The paper reports Spearman correlation and Kendall's Tau alongside it to assess monotonic agreement and rank-order consistency.

metrics.name: Spearman correlation
metrics.caveat: The paper reports Pearson correlation and Kendall's Tau alongside it.

metrics.name: Kendall's Tau
metrics.caveat: The paper reports Pearson and Spearman correlations alongside it.

controls.name: Random guessing
controls.detail: A random-choice condition is evaluated alongside the VLMs; the paper gives 25% chance accuracy for four-choice questions and reports task-specific random scores for Q2.
controls.rules_out: Performance being attributable to chance-level selection alone.

confounds.name: Benchmark-to-real-world correlation may depend on the shared predefined-option setup
confounds.detail: The benchmark result and real-world result could correlate because both ask VLMs to select from predefined options, rather than because benchmark performance predicts general real-world action-generation ability.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out in these experiments. The authors explicitly acknowledge the shared option-selection setup as a limitation and identify direct action generation as a future direction.

evidence_standards.name: Correlation significance and complementary rank correlations
evidence_standards.detail: For benchmark-to-real-world alignment, the paper reports Pearson's r = 0.889 (p = 0.003), Spearman's rho = 0.850 (p = 0.007), and Kendall's Tau = 0.691 (p = 0.018), and treats p < 0.05 as statistically significant.

evidence_standards.name: Human evaluation
evidence_standards.detail: Thirty-six volunteers each answer a subset of 50–70 questions for each question type; their accuracies are used to obtain the human score.

evidence_standards.name: Real-world trial repetitions
evidence_standards.detail: The seven real-world tasks are each run for three trials, and success rates are reported.

evidence_standards.name: Variation across fabric dimensions
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports standard deviations of model accuracies across fabric-manipulation dimensions; it does not state a threshold for deciding that differences are real.

datasets.name: YCB Object and Model Set
datasets.eval_protocol: Physical YCB objects are used in the example manipulation protocols; the paper specifies task-specific object subsets and setups, with no general train/test split.

datasets.name: Pitcher-Mug Benchmark
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the YCB pitcher and mug in 10 specified initial configurations. Scores penalize liquid remaining in the pitcher or spilled on the table; the robot succeeds in 8 of 10 configurations.

datasets.name: YCB Gripper Assessment Benchmark
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses objects from the YCB shape and tool categories and scores gripper performance with a scoring table. Evaluated on the Model T and Model T42 grippers; no trial count is stated in the provided text.

datasets.name: Table Setting Benchmark
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the YCB mug, fork, knife, spoon, bowl, and plate, placed at predefined initial locations and moved to specified final configurations. Scores accuracy of the final object poses.

datasets.name: Block Pick and Place Benchmark
datasets.eval_protocol: Tests grasping small blocks and transferring them to specified locations; awards points based on task completion and placement precision. No trial count is stated in the provided text.

datasets.name: Peg Insertion Learning Assessment Benchmark
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates a learned peg-insertion controller under random-direction peg-board position perturbations, including 5 mm and 10 mm. Reports 4 successes in 10 trials at 5 mm and complete failure at 10 mm; the 5 mm result is reported for a 1-second controller execution.

datasets.name: Box and Blocks Test
datasets.eval_protocol: On a PR2, repeatedly samples a location uniformly over the box, attempts a pick, and detects a grasp by checking whether the gripper closes fully. Runs 10 experiments of 2 minutes each; performance is the number of blocks moved to the other side.

metrics.name: Liquid remaining in pitcher and liquid spilled on table

datasets.name: CMU MoCap
datasets.eval_protocol: The paper selects 780 clips for training, filtering for single-person motions on flat terrain and excluding motions involving interactions, heavy objects, or rough terrain. In simulation it evaluates 10,000 trajectories across 4,096 environments, sampling movement goals from retargeted motions or uniformly from the stated random-command range, and reports mean episode metrics. Real-world tests use the listed expressive motion clips; the paper does not specify a train/test split.

baselines.name: ExBody + AMP
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated in the same simulation protocol as ExBody (10,000 trajectories across 4,096 environments) and compared using the same episode metrics; no further matching or tuning details are stated.

baselines.name: ExBody + AMP NoReg
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated in the same simulation protocol as ExBody (10,000 trajectories across 4,096 environments) and compared using the same episode metrics; no further matching or tuning details are stated.

metrics.name: Mean Episode Linear Velocity Tracking Reward (MELV)
Mean episode roll pitch tracking reward (MERP)
Mean episode lengths (MEL)
metrics.caveat: A high MEL can reflect a stable kneeling behavior that ignores the movement goal; the paper reports MELV and MEK alongside it.

metrics.name: Mean episode key body tracking reward (MEK)
Mean absolute roll and pitch angle
metrics.caveat: The paper uses this as an indicator of real-world stability, not as a direct motion-tracking measure.

controls.name: Random Sample
controls.detail: Uniformly samples root movement goals from the stated range instead of sampling them from retargeted motions.
controls.rules_out: A difference tests whether the motion-dataset goal distribution, rather than just training on sampled goals, benefits policy learning.

controls.name: No RSI
controls.detail: Initializes environments from default DoF positions and root states instead of states sampled from the motion dataset.
controls.rules_out: A difference supports the contribution of motion-data-based state initialization to exploration and learning.

controls.name: Full Body Tracking
controls.detail: Tracks lower-body joint angles and keypoints as well as the upper body, rather than relaxing lower-body imitation.
controls.rules_out: A difference tests whether relaxing lower-body tracking improves the reported performance.

controls.name: ExBody + AMP NoReg
controls.detail: Removes the regularization terms from the reward while using the AMP reward.
controls.rules_out: A difference tests whether AMP alone can replace the regularization terms.

confounds.name: High episode length reflects kneeling rather than following the movement goal
confounds.detail: The Random Sample policy can exploit the environment by kneeling immediately, producing a stable behavior and a high episode length while ignoring the root movement goal.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports MELV and MEK alongside MEL; the Random Sample condition has poor movement-velocity and key-body tracking rewards, and the kneeling behavior is shown in Fig. 8.

evidence_standards.name: Simulation aggregation
evidence_standards.detail: Reports mean episode metrics over 10,000 trajectories in 4,096 environments. The paper does not report seeds, variance, confidence intervals, statistical tests, or a numerical threshold for calling differences real.

evidence_standards.name: Real-world roll and pitch measurements
evidence_standards.detail: Reports mean absolute roll and pitch angles for a 10-second test per motion. The paper does not state repeated-run counts, uncertainty, or a statistical test.

datasets.name: Open Messaging Benchmark
datasets.eval_protocol: The paper follows its latency definition using a synthetic 2048-byte payload across five RIO middleware backends and 1,000 passes; latency is half the median round-trip time, with the 1st and 99th percentiles removed.

baselines.name: LeRobot
baselines.fair_comparison: Run action chunks from the same fine-tuned π 0.5 policy with an SO-100 in the loop and an identical camera setup; the paper says robot read/write overhead is negligible relative to observation capture, inference, and action execution.

metrics.name: Success rate
metrics.caveat: For the T-shirt folding task, half points were awarded for each fold.

metrics.name: Task completion time
metrics.caveat: Rollout-time retries can lengthen completion time; the paper attributes the bimanual gap from demonstration time to policies retrying rather than to system overhead.

confounds.name: The latency difference from LeRobot could be due to different camera or robot-loop conditions
confounds.detail: A camera setup difference or robot read/write overhead could explain the observation-to-action latency comparison without a benefit from RIO’s pipeline.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The comparison uses the same fine-tuned π 0.5 policy, action chunks, SO-100 in the loop, and camera setup; the paper reports robot read/write overhead as negligible relative to observation capture, inference, and action execution.

evidence_standards.name: Real-robot policy evaluations use 20 trials
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports success rates across 20 trials; task completion times are reported as averages with ± values, without specifying a statistical test or a threshold for treating differences as real.

evidence_standards.name: Middleware latency uses 1,000 passes
evidence_standards.detail: Latency is reported as mean ± standard deviation; the paper does not specify a statistical test or a threshold for treating differences as real.

baselines.name: Peng et al. latent-space method
baselines.fair_comparison: All methods were pretrained with dynamics randomization on flat ground until convergence; the same 10 environment instantiations were used for all methods. The method used SAC as its training-time policy optimizer to match the paper’s method.

baselines.name: RMA
baselines.fair_comparison: All methods were pretrained with dynamics randomization on flat ground until convergence; the same 10 environment instantiations were used for all methods. RMA used SAC as its training-time policy optimizer to match the paper’s method.

baselines.name: SAC
baselines.fair_comparison: This ablation uses vanilla SAC instead of REDQ for both pretraining and fine-tuning. Both fine-tuning methods collect an initial buffer before fine-tuning.

controls.name: Pretrained policy before real-world fine-tuning
controls.detail: The policy is evaluated before and after fine-tuning; deterministic policies are used for these evaluations.
controls.rules_out: That the post-training performance is simply the pretrained policy’s performance, and supports attributing the difference to fine-tuning.

controls.name: SAC ablation
controls.detail: Uses vanilla SAC instead of REDQ for both pretraining and fine-tuning.
controls.rules_out: That the reported benefit of REDQ is merely a benefit of fine-tuning in general rather than the choice of REDQ.

evidence_standards.name: Mean and standard deviation across 10 trials
evidence_standards.detail: Simulation adaptation performance is reported across 10 trials; real-world deterministic-policy evaluations before and after fine-tuning are reported over 10 trials.

evidence_standards.name: Stochastic training policy and deterministic evaluation policy
evidence_standards.detail: Average return during training is collected from a stochastic policy; before-and-after evaluations use a deterministic policy.

datasets.name: Pitcher-Mug Protocol and Benchmark
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the YCB pitcher and mug in ten specified initial configurations; scores by penalizing liquid remaining in the pitcher or spilled on the table. The reported implementation succeeds in 8 of 10 configurations.

datasets.name: YCB Gripper Assessment Protocol and Benchmark
datasets.eval_protocol: Tests grippers on objects from the YCB shape and tool categories using a scoring table; the paper applies it to the Model T and Model T42 grippers.

datasets.name: YCB Table Setting Protocol and Benchmark
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the YCB mug, fork, knife, spoon, bowl, and plate at predefined initial locations; scores the accuracy of the final object poses.

datasets.name: Block Pick and Place Protocol and Benchmark
datasets.eval_protocol: Tests transferring small blocks to specified locations; awards points for task completion and manipulation precision. The paper reports a HERB implementation.

datasets.name: Peg Insertion Learning Assessment Protocol and Benchmark
datasets.eval_protocol: Tests a learned linear-Gaussian controller on a PR2 with the peg board displaced in a random direction by 5 mm or 10 mm; reports 4 successes in 10 trials at 5 mm and failure at 10 mm. The controller is run for one second for the reported 5 mm result.

datasets.name: Box and Blocks Test
datasets.eval_protocol: Runs the PR2 for 10 experiments of 2 minutes each. The robot repeatedly samples a location uniformly over the box and attempts to pick and transfer a block; reports the number of blocks moved.

metrics.name: Blocks transferred in the Box and Blocks Test
Binary task success/failure
metrics.caveat: The paper recommends avoiding binary measures where possible and scoring intermediate task steps with partial points instead.

datasets.name: Go1 forward locomotion
datasets.eval_protocol: Train in simulation for a 2 m/s forward-velocity task; evaluate in the real world on a 5 m lab track, measuring forward projected velocity and distance traveled. The robustness evaluation additionally tests artificial turf, socks on the robot’s legs, and an outdoor sidewalk. The paper trains 16 DrEureka DR configurations and uses 3 random seeds per configuration.

datasets.name: LEAP hand cube rotation
datasets.eval_protocol: Train in simulation to rotate a cube in-hand, then evaluate real-world cube rotation during a 20-second interval; report total rotation and time-to-fall. The policy observes joint angles and proprioceptive history, not cube pose. The paper uses 16 DrEureka DR configurations and 3 random seeds per configuration.

datasets.name: Go1 walking globe
datasets.eval_protocol: Train in simulation to balance and walk on a yoga ball; report time on the ball in simulation and in the real world. The lab evaluation uses a human-held center support and restricts the ball to a 1 m radius; the paper also reports qualitative outdoor tests on varied terrain and perturbations.

baselines.name: Human-Designed
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the original task implementations’ human-designed reward and DR configurations. Policy-training hyperparameters are not modified or tuned for DrEureka; for locomotion, the baseline is trained with its velocity curriculum and evaluated at 2 m/s.

baselines.name: Eureka
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses LLM-generated rewards without safety consideration and trains without domain randomization. The paper also compares it with DrEureka without DR to isolate the safety-instruction effect.

baselines.name: CEM Random
baselines.fair_comparison: CEM starts at simulation-default parameter values with variance 1; run for 4 iterations with 4 samples each, matching the 16-sample budget.

baselines.name: CEM RAPP
baselines.fair_comparison: CEM is initialized by randomly sampling within RAPP bounds and run for 4 iterations with 4 samples each, matching the 16-sample budget.

baselines.name: BayRn RAPP
baselines.fair_comparison: Parameters are bounded by RAPP and initial samples are drawn randomly within RAPP. Uses 8 initial samples and 8 further iterations, matching the 16-sample budget; uses a Matérn 2.5 kernel and UCB with κ=5 and ξ=1.

metrics.name: Cube rotation (rad)
metrics.caveat: The authors say the task allows little room for error, so policies tend to perform very well or very badly, producing relatively large standard deviations; they report time-to-fall alongside rotation.

controls.name: No DR
controls.detail: Uses the DrEureka reward but trains without domain randomization.
controls.rules_out: Whether DrEureka’s performance can be attributed to adding domain randomization rather than the reward alone.

controls.name: Human-Designed DR with DrEureka reward
controls.detail: Fixes the reward to DrEureka’s reward and uses the original human-designed DR configuration.
controls.rules_out: Whether the result is explained simply by using a human-designed DR configuration rather than DrEureka’s generated configuration.

controls.name: Prompt DR
controls.detail: Uses the full RAPP parameter-prior ranges directly as the DR configuration, with the DrEureka reward fixed.
controls.rules_out: Whether directly applying the feasible RAPP ranges is sufficient, rather than having the LLM choose narrower ranges.

controls.name: No Prior
controls.detail: The LLM receives the parameter names but no RAPP ranges; the DrEureka reward is fixed.
controls.rules_out: Whether the LLM’s DR generation works as well without reward-aware parameter priors.

controls.name: Uninformative Prior
controls.detail: The LLM receives broad default search ranges rather than reward-aware RAPP ranges; the DrEureka reward is fixed.
controls.rules_out: Whether the result depends on informative reward-aware bounds rather than merely supplying ranges.

controls.name: Random Sampling
controls.detail: Randomly samples DR configurations within RAPP ranges, with the DrEureka reward fixed.
controls.rules_out: Whether any samples from the RAPP ranges work as well as LLM-generated configurations.

controls.name: DrEureka without safety instruction
controls.detail: For the safety ablation, compares the no-safety Eureka reward against DrEureka without DR, removing DR as an explanation for the reward comparison.
controls.rules_out: Whether the transfer result is due to the safety instruction in reward generation rather than domain randomization.

controls.name: Fixed Human-Designed DR for reward comparison
controls.detail: Retrains DrEureka and human-written reward policies with the same Human-Designed DR; also evaluates the human-written reward with a fixed 2 m/s target instead of its velocity curriculum.
controls.rules_out: Whether reward-function differences explain the simulation training comparison, rather than DR differences or the human reward’s curriculum.

confounds.name: LLM data leakage from open-source task code or human-designed ranges
confounds.detail: The LLM could have seen the tasks and human-designed ranges and generate reasonable ranges even when the prompt withholds RAPP priors.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The No Prior condition performs very poorly in real-world locomotion despite access to the parameter names; the authors take this as evidence that data leakage does not explain the result.

confounds.name: The human holding the globe-task leash provides upward support
confounds.detail: Apparent balancing on the yoga ball could be aided by a person lifting or supporting the robot.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors state that the leash is held parallel to the ground to avoid upward force and is used only to keep the robot within a safe radius.

confounds.name: High simulation performance reflects unsafe or unnatural behavior rather than transferable behavior
confounds.detail: A policy can score well in simulation by exploiting the simulator or learning unsafe behavior, while failing in real deployment.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper evaluates policies in the real world; its no-safety Eureka comparison moves quickly in simulation but face-plants in deployment, while the safety-instruction condition transfers.

confounds.name: Broad DR ranges cause excessive motor effort rather than robust transfer
confounds.detail: Prompt DR’s wide ranges could make policies over-exert forces, explaining its poorer real-world outcome.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors compare real-world hip-torque histograms for DrEureka and Prompt DR policies and report lower torque for DrEureka policies.

evidence_standards.name: Three random seeds per DR configuration; report mean and standard deviation
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports averages and standard deviations across trials and seeds. For DrEureka it evaluates 16 DR configurations and reports both the best and average real-world performance. No formal statistical test or threshold for declaring a difference real is specified.

datasets.name: BridgeData V2
datasets.eval_protocol: WidowX evaluation on 17 tasks with 10 trials per task (170 rollouts per approach); A/B evaluations use the same tasks and initial robot/object states. Reports success rate. For quantization, evaluates 8 representative tasks with 80 rollouts per precision setting. For parameter-efficient fine-tuning, evaluates selected Franka-Tabletop tasks with 33 rollouts per approach. The paper also reports five language-grounding tasks in a BridgeData V2 sink environment for its backbone experiments.

datasets.name: Google robot
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates 12 tasks with 5 trials per task (60 rollouts per approach); A/B evaluations use the same tasks and initial robot/object states. Reports success rate.

datasets.name: Franka-Tabletop
datasets.eval_protocol: Fine-tunes on 10–150 demonstrations per target task using a 5 Hz non-blocking controller. Evaluates as part of seven Franka tasks across both Franka setups, with 99 Franka-Tabletop rollouts per approach; selected tasks use 33 rollouts per approach in the parameter-efficient fine-tuning comparison. Reports success rate.

datasets.name: Franka-DROID
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the Franka setup from the DROID dataset, mounted on a movable standing desk, with a 15 Hz non-blocking controller; fine-tunes on 10–150 demonstrations per target task. Evaluates with 30 rollouts per approach as part of the seven-task Franka evaluation. Reports success rate.

baselines.name: RT-1-X
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same tasks and initial robot/object states as OpenVLA in the A/B evaluations.

baselines.name: RT-2-X
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same tasks and initial robot/object states as OpenVLA in the A/B evaluations.

baselines.name: Octo
baselines.fair_comparison: For out-of-the-box evaluations, evaluated on the same tasks and initial robot/object states as OpenVLA. For fine-tuning evaluations, fine-tuned on the same target dataset as OpenVLA.

baselines.name: Diffusion Policy
baselines.fair_comparison: Trained from scratch on the seven Franka tasks using the same target-task data (10–150 demonstrations per task). Its full setup uses two-step image and proprioceptive observation history and action chunking; the paper reports these specification differences.

baselines.name: Diffusion Policy (matched)
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the same input/output specifications as OpenVLA: a single image, no proprioception or observation history, and one relative-position action without action chunking.

metrics.name: Success rate
metrics.caveat: For 8-bit quantized inference, real-world success can be affected by the low inference rate and resulting change in system dynamics, rather than only by policy accuracy; the paper reports inference frequency and offline action-token accuracy alongside success.

metrics.name: Action-token accuracy
metrics.caveat: Offline token accuracy does not by itself capture real-world performance under changed system dynamics; the paper compares it with real-world rollout success and inference frequency.

controls.name: OpenVLA (scratch)
controls.detail: Directly fine-tunes the base Prismatic VLM on the target robot setup instead of fine-tuning the OpenX-pretrained OpenVLA model.
controls.rules_out: A downstream-task gain being due only to fine-tuning the base VLM, rather than benefiting from OpenX robot pretraining.

controls.name: bfloat16 inference
controls.detail: The default, non-quantized inference condition compared with int8 and int4 on the same representative BridgeData V2 tasks.
controls.rules_out: A quantized model’s performance being interpreted without comparison to the standard-precision inference condition.

confounds.name: Diffusion Policy’s different observation and action specifications explain performance differences
confounds.detail: The full Diffusion Policy uses observation history and proprioception and predicts action chunks, unlike OpenVLA; these differences could account for a comparison result independently of the policy approach.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper also evaluates Diffusion Policy (matched), which uses a single image, no proprioception or observation history, and a single relative-position action without action chunking.

confounds.name: Quantization-related accuracy loss, rather than slow inference, explains the 8-bit real-world performance drop
confounds.detail: A lower real-world success rate with 8-bit inference could be attributed to inaccurate quantized predictions rather than to the changed control dynamics caused by slow inference.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports comparable offline token accuracy for 8-bit and 4-bit inference versus bfloat16, while measuring that 8-bit runs at only 1.2 Hz on the evaluation GPU and changes the dynamics of the 5 Hz controller.

evidence_standards.name: Mean success rate with standard error
evidence_standards.detail: Real-robot rollout success rates are reported as mean ± StdErr.

evidence_standards.name: A/B evaluation with matched initial conditions
evidence_standards.detail: Comparisons use the same tasks and the same sets of initial robot and object states for each approach.

baselines.name: Blind-WBC
baselines.fair_comparison: The underlying blind WBC directly executes the target command; it is the lower-performance reference.

baselines.name: Teachers
baselines.fair_comparison: Privileged teachers used to train the students; treated as an upper-bound reference.

baselines.name: PointNet
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the same recurrent policy, teacher labels, and distillation setup as RECAL; only the geometry encoder and corresponding observation representation change.

baselines.name: Voxel
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the same recurrent policy, teacher labels, and distillation setup as RECAL; only the geometry encoder and corresponding observation representation change.

metrics.name: Collision-free success (CF)
metrics.caveat: It is a binary episode-level measure and does not distinguish collision severity; the paper also reports average collision-force magnitude by body region.

metrics.name: Tracking deviation (Dev)
metrics.caveat: Computed only on safe trajectory states, so low deviation can coexist with tracking through contact; the paper reports CF and collision-force magnitude alongside it. Locomotion uses planar velocity error, and reaching uses Euclidean hand-to-target distance.

metrics.name: Average collision-force magnitude
metrics.caveat: Force magnitude alone does not indicate whether an episode was collision-free; the paper reports it alongside CF and breaks it down by body region for the hardest settings.

controls.name: Blind-WBC reference
controls.detail: The underlying WBC executes the target command directly, without RECAL.
controls.rules_out: That the reported collision-avoidance improvement is already achieved by the unmodified WBC.

controls.name: PointNet geometry-encoder comparison
controls.detail: Replaces RECAL’s query-conditioned cross-attention encoder while keeping the recurrent policy, teacher labels, and distillation setup the same.
controls.rules_out: That the result follows simply from adding a geometry encoder, rather than from RECAL’s robot-centric cross-attention design.

controls.name: Voxel geometry-encoder comparison
controls.detail: Replaces RECAL’s encoder with a voxel-based encoder while keeping the recurrent policy, teacher labels, and distillation setup the same.
controls.rules_out: That the result follows simply from adding a geometry encoder, rather than from RECAL’s robot-centric cross-attention design.

confounds.name: Low tracking deviation could come from tracking commands through contact
confounds.detail: A controller could appear to track well while continuing unsafe motion through collisions.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Dev is computed only on safe trajectory states; the paper reports CF and body-region collision-force magnitude alongside it.

confounds.name: Voxel’s weaker results could reflect insufficient training or tuning rather than its encoder
confounds.detail: The paper notes that longer training or additional hyperparameter tuning might improve Voxel.
confounds.ruled_out_by: It reports that Voxel was trained for over five times as many steps as RECAL, but acknowledges that further tuning may still improve it; this explanation is not fully ruled out.

evidence_standards.name: 5 seeds; results averaged
evidence_standards.detail: Table I reports results averaged over 5 seeds. The paper does not specify variance estimates, a statistical test, or a threshold for treating differences as real.

controls.name: w/o S1
controls.detail: Skip the footwork-acquisition stage; this setting terminates before its first hitting trial.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the full result can be obtained without first learning locomotion; this run did not yield a meaningful hitting evaluation.

controls.name: w/o S1 w/ lower entropy coefficient
controls.detail: Skip S1 and reduce the entropy coefficient to obtain feasible hitting behavior.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether reducing exploration can compensate for omitting S1; it achieves lower success and racket speed than the full method.

controls.name: w/o S2
controls.detail: Remove the precision-guided swing-generation stage; also evaluated on boundary-region hits.
controls.rules_out: Tests the contribution of S2; the larger success-rate drop on boundary hits supports its role in challenging long-distance interceptions.

controls.name: w/o S3
controls.detail: Omit task-focused refinement, including its removal of gait-shaping terms and its domain randomization and observation noise.
controls.rules_out: Tests the contribution of the final refinement stage; comparison shows whether its changes affect motion regularization and performance.

controls.name: Prediction-Free
controls.detail: Replace commanded target position, orientation, and time with the current shuttle position and five previous position frames; keep the reward, action space, and curriculum unchanged.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the target-known observation is needed for hitting performance and measures the effect of removing explicit target information.

confounds.name: Performance may depend on accurately known aerodynamic parameters
confounds.detail: The EKF prediction could be effective only when the aerodynamic characteristic length used by the model is accurate.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Perturb the aerodynamic characteristic length by ±20% and measure prediction accuracy; accuracy decreases, but the authors report it remains acceptable.

evidence_standards.name: Five independent random-seed runs; report mean and standard deviation
evidence_standards.detail: For simulation ablations, each setting is evaluated over five runs with different random seeds, and results are reported as mean ± standard deviation across the five seeds.

baselines.name: Fine-tune π(s)
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the same arm policy as RTR: XY Compliant + Z Schedule.

baselines.name: Fine-tune Δπ(s)
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the same arm policy as RTR: XY Compliant + Z Schedule; the base policy is frozen and the residual policy is initialized with its last-layer weights reset to zero.

metrics.name: Walking tracking reward / treadmill speed
metrics.caveat: The robot’s global-frame velocity is near zero on the treadmill, so treadmill speed is used as a proxy for walking speed; torso pitch and roll and end-effector forces are also reported to assess walking stability.

metrics.name: End-effector force X, Y, and Z
Swing-up force amplitude at the dominant frequency

controls.name: XY Fixed + Z Schedule
controls.detail: For the arm-compliance ablation, the arm remains stationary in XY and follows the height schedule; compliance is re-enabled during evaluation.
controls.rules_out: A benefit explained by the arm-height schedule alone rather than XY compliance.

controls.name: XY Compliant + Z High (Easy)
controls.detail: Trains with the arm at a relatively high height (Δ = 0 m) and evaluates at a lower height (Δ = −0.02 m).
controls.rules_out: That high training reward under strong arm support necessarily reflects a policy that performs when support is reduced.

controls.name: XY Compliant + Z Low (Hard)
controls.detail: Uses the low arm height (Δ = −0.02 m) during both training and evaluation.
controls.rules_out: That RTR’s result is explained simply by training and evaluating at the same arm height.

controls.name: Freeze π(s)
controls.detail: Keeps the policy fixed rather than fine-tuning it; uses the same arm policy as RTR.
controls.rules_out: That the observed adaptation occurs without policy fine-tuning.

controls.name: Fine-tune π(s)
controls.detail: Fine-tunes the original policy directly, using the same arm policy as RTR.
controls.rules_out: That any real-world policy fine-tuning gives the same result as fine-tuning the dynamics latent.

controls.name: Fine-tune Δπ(s)
controls.detail: Freezes the base policy and trains a residual policy initialized with its last-layer weights reset to zero; uses the same arm policy as RTR.
controls.rules_out: That residual-policy fine-tuning gives the same result as latent fine-tuning.

controls.name: Freeze π(s,z)
controls.detail: Keeps the dynamics-conditioned policy fixed rather than fine-tuning its latent.
controls.rules_out: That the dynamics-conditioned policy achieves the result without real-world latent fine-tuning.

controls.name: Fixed arm in swing-up
controls.detail: Keeps the arm fixed during the swing-up training schedule.
controls.rules_out: That active arm involvement is unnecessary for the reported learning improvement.

controls.name: Perturbing arm in swing-up
controls.detail: Uses phase-inverted arm motion to damp the swing during selected schedule bins.
controls.rules_out: That only an arm schedule that actively helps the swing can improve over a fixed arm.

controls.name: Helping arm without a pretrained critic
controls.detail: Uses the helping arm schedule but omits critic pretraining on offline data.
controls.rules_out: That the early learning improvement is independent of critic pretraining.

confounds.name: High reward may come from arm support rather than a policy that performs with less support
confounds.detail: A policy trained with the arm held high could exploit the support, making its training curve look good even if performance collapses when support is reduced.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The Z High (Easy) condition is evaluated at a lower arm height (Δ = −0.02 m); its performance collapses at evaluation, exposing the training–evaluation gap.

evidence_standards.name: Three random seeds; mean and standard deviation
evidence_standards.detail: The walking ablation and swing-up experiments are each run with three random seeds, and plots show the mean and standard deviation; no statistical test or significance threshold is specified.

baselines.name: Source RL policy (AMP)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared in the same fixed target environment and randomized target environment as the Diffusion Policies; the source policy is evaluated in 100 runs in the fixed environment and 100 randomized target environments.

controls.name: No-randomization data-collection condition
controls.detail: Diffusion Policies are trained on datasets collected without data-collection randomization, at the same dataset sizes as the randomized-data conditions.
controls.rules_out: A performance difference against randomized-data conditions cannot be attributed solely to dataset size; it supports an effect of data-collection randomization at a matched size.

confounds.name: Performance gains are due to dataset size rather than dataset diversity
confounds.detail: A larger dataset could improve performance regardless of the randomization used during collection.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate three dataset sizes (500K, 2M, and 8M transitions) across the collection conditions and compare randomization conditions at matched sizes; the paper reports that size alone does not compensate for insufficient diversity.

evidence_standards.name: Three random seeds per Diffusion Policy; results reported with ± values
evidence_standards.detail: The paper does not specify what the ± values represent and reports no statistical test or threshold for treating differences as real.

datasets.name: Barkour
datasets.eval_protocol: Real-robot full-course evaluation: 71 specialist-policy runs and 19 Locomotion-Transformer runs; timing starts when the torso center leaves the start table and stops when the robot climbs onto the end table. A trial is valid if the robot stands on the end table for 5 seconds. Score is 1.0 minus 0.01 per full second over the allotted time and 0.1 per failed or skipped obstacle. The paper also reports individual-obstacle specialist results and PyBullet simulation Barkour scores for ablations.

controls.name: MLP policy trained on the same dataset
controls.detail: A larger version of the specialist-policy architecture is trained on the Locomotion-Transformer dataset and evaluated in simulation.
controls.rules_out: Whether the reported distilled-policy performance depends on using the Transformer rather than simply distilling the same data into an MLP.

controls.name: Single multi-task RL policy
controls.detail: One policy is trained with a mixed terrain curriculum: 50% slope, 30% uneven terrain, and 20% gap data, using the omnidirectional walking reward.
controls.rules_out: Whether specialist training is necessary to solve the distinct Barkour skills; the policy walks the start table and weave poles but fails the A-frame and broad jump.

evidence_standards.name: Reported variation and runs
evidence_standards.detail: Hardware results are reported as mean and one standard deviation; the full-course specialist evaluation has 71 runs and the Locomotion-Transformer evaluation has 19 trials. Simulation ablations use three random seeds and report the mean and standard deviation of the mean evaluation scores. No statistical test or threshold for treating differences as real is specified.

datasets.name: Robomimic (Can and Square; PH and MH variants)
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses proficient-human (PH) and mixed proficient/non-proficient-human (MH) demonstrations: 200 PH and 300 MH demonstrations for each task. Reports success rate; simulation evaluation averages results across 3 training seeds and 50 environment initializations, using the average of the last 10 checkpoints (saved every 50 epochs) alongside maximum performance in the reported format.

datasets.name: Tilt
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses 200 automated-program demonstrations; initial cube position and size vary. Reports success rate across 3 training seeds and 50 environment initializations, with maximum performance and the average of the last 10 checkpoints reported.

datasets.name: Push-T
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses 200 PH demonstrations; initial block and end-effector conditions vary. Reports target area coverage (rather than success rate) across 3 training seeds and 50 environment initializations, with maximum performance and the average of the last 10 checkpoints reported.

datasets.name: Move-T (real-world)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates policies trained on push-only (128 demonstrations), grasp-only (64), and combined-mode (192) datasets, with 20 test runs per method for each dataset. Reports stage-specific success and IoU; stage 1 counts when the IoU criterion is met, and stage 2 requires IoU above 0.8 and the end-effector reaching the end-zone. IoU is measured at the final step, not maximized over steps.

datasets.name: Cloth Unfold (real-world)
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses 100 demonstrations and tests each method 50 times; reports success rate and failure counts.

baselines.name: Diffusion Policy
baselines.fair_comparison: For simulation comparisons, the paper uses a reduced-size CNN-based Diffusion Policy with the same backbone as HDP to accelerate training, and reproduces its state-based-input results on all benchmarks. In the real-world Move-T comparison, both methods are evaluated on the same demonstration-mode datasets.

metrics.name: IoU
metrics.caveat: For Move-T, measuring the maximum IoU over steps would not reflect the final task state; the paper measures IoU at the last step and also reports stage-specific success rates.

controls.name: HDP (No-OC)
controls.detail: Removes objective-contact conditioning; the Actor is conditioned only on observations.
controls.rules_out: A gain over this condition supports a contribution from contact guidance rather than HDP's other components alone.

controls.name: HDP (eta=0)
controls.detail: Sets the Q-learning coefficient to zero while retaining the rest of the HDP setup.
controls.rules_out: A difference from HDP with Q-learning enabled tests whether the Q-learning objective contributes beyond imitation learning.

controls.name: Nearest-objective-contact scheme
controls.detail: Uses the immediate contact as the objective, rather than phased objective contacts.
controls.rules_out: A difference from the phased scheme tests whether filtering misoperations and configuring phased contacts matters, beyond simply using contact guidance.

controls.name: Iterative denoising
controls.detail: Uses iterative denoising instead of the paper's one-step snapshot-gradient optimization for the Actor update.
controls.rules_out: A difference tests whether the reported optimization benefit depends on snapshot-gradient optimization rather than iterative denoising.

controls.name: Alternative 3D encoder conditions
controls.detail: Compares the proposed encoder with no 3D encoder, PointNet, PointNet without batch normalization, PointNet++, and PointNet++ without batch normalization.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the encoder results are specific to the proposed encoder and its handling of normalization, rather than following from adding any 3D encoder.

confounds.name: The apparent benefit of contact guidance could instead come from the 3D encoder
confounds.detail: A direct comparison of HDP with Diffusion Policy changes both contact conditioning and the observation encoder; the paper notes that HDP (No-OC) versus Diffusion Policy differs by the added 3D encoder.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare HDP with objective contacts against HDP (No-OC), which removes contact conditioning while retaining the HDP setup.

confounds.name: The benefit of phased contacts could come from contact guidance generally, rather than filtering demonstration misoperations
confounds.detail: Both phased and immediate-contact schemes provide objective-contact guidance, so their difference tests the claimed benefit of filtering misoperations and configuring phased contacts.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate phased objective contacts against the nearest-objective-contact scheme and report the success-rate comparison.

evidence_standards.name: Simulation evaluation runs and checkpoint reporting
evidence_standards.detail: Reports maximum performance and average performance over the last 10 checkpoints, saved every 50 epochs; results are averaged across 3 training seeds and 50 environment initializations. No statistical test or significance threshold is specified.

evidence_standards.name: Real-world Move-T test runs
evidence_standards.detail: Reports results from 20 test runs per method for each of the three demonstration-mode datasets.

evidence_standards.name: Real-world Cloth Unfold test runs
evidence_standards.detail: Tests each method 50 times and reports success rate and failure counts.

datasets.name: LIBERO-Spatial
datasets.eval_protocol: 10-task suite; evaluated sequentially using success-rate-based FWT, NBT, and AUC, with success rates assessed at epochs 0, 5, ..., 50; results averaged over three seeds. No evaluation episode count is stated.

datasets.name: LIBERO-Object
datasets.eval_protocol: 10-task suite; evaluated sequentially using success-rate-based FWT, NBT, and AUC, with success rates assessed at epochs 0, 5, ..., 50; results averaged over three seeds. No evaluation episode count is stated.

datasets.name: LIBERO-Goal
datasets.eval_protocol: 10-task suite; evaluated sequentially using success-rate-based FWT, NBT, and AUC, with success rates assessed at epochs 0, 5, ..., 50; results averaged over three seeds. No evaluation episode count is stated.

datasets.name: LIBERO-Long
datasets.eval_protocol: 10 long-horizon tasks from LIBERO-100; downstream lifelong-learning evaluation using success-rate-based FWT, NBT, and AUC, with success rates assessed at epochs 0, 5, ..., 50; results averaged over three seeds. No evaluation episode count is stated.

datasets.name: LIBERO-90
datasets.eval_protocol: 90 short-horizon tasks from LIBERO-100 used for behavioral-cloning pretraining for 50 epochs; checkpoints saved every 5 epochs, with the best-performing checkpoint for each architecture selected for downstream evaluation on LIBERO-Long.

baselines.name: SeqL (sequential finetuning)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with lifelong-learning algorithms using the same ResNet-T policy architecture; algorithm-comparison results are averaged over three seeds.

baselines.name: ER (Experience Replay)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with other lifelong-learning algorithms using the same ResNet-T policy architecture; algorithm-comparison results are averaged over three seeds.

baselines.name: EWC (Elastic Weight Consolidation)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with other lifelong-learning algorithms using the same ResNet-T policy architecture; algorithm-comparison results are averaged over three seeds.

baselines.name: PackNet
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with other lifelong-learning algorithms using the same ResNet-T policy architecture; algorithm-comparison results are averaged over three seeds.

baselines.name: MTL (multitask learning)
baselines.fair_comparison: Included as an upper-bound reference in the algorithm comparison with the policy fixed to ResNet-T; results are averaged over three seeds.

metrics.name: Success rate
metrics.caveat: The paper says success rate is more reliable than training loss for manipulation policies, and uses success rate to compute FWT, NBT, and AUC.

controls.name: Task-ID embedding
controls.detail: Compared with pretrained language embeddings using ResNet-T and ER on LIBERO-Long; the Task-ID embedding is produced by feeding a string such as “Task 5” into pretrained BERT.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether semantically rich task descriptions provide an advantage over an embedding that identifies the task without its semantic description.

controls.name: Training from scratch (no pretraining)
controls.detail: Compared with models pretrained by behavioral cloning on LIBERO-90 before downstream lifelong learning on LIBERO-Long.
controls.rules_out: Shows whether downstream results differ from a model that did not receive the pretraining intervention.

evidence_standards.name: Three seeds; mean and standard error
evidence_standards.detail: Main tables report results averaged over three seeds with the mean and standard error.

evidence_standards.name: Two-tailed Student’s t-test
evidence_standards.detail: For table comparisons, statistical significance is assessed using a two-tailed Student’s t-test with equal sample sizes and unequal variance, at p = 0.05.

evidence_standards.name: Five task orderings; standard deviation
evidence_standards.detail: The task-order study evaluates five orderings and shows standard deviation for a fixed ordering; the paper reports a statistically significant ordering effect for PackNet.

datasets.name: 2D maze (GCS and RRT trajectories)
datasets.eval_protocol: 50 smooth GCS trajectories form the target data and 5,000 jittery RRT trajectories the suboptimal data. Evaluate on 1,000 trials with random start and goal positions; success means reaching an ε-ball around the goal within the time limit without collision. Report success rate and average squared acceleration.

datasets.name: 7-DoF neural motion planning
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate on 1,000 trials; start and goal configurations are sampled around objects and shelves, and the planner predicts the plan open-loop. Success means completing the motion-planning task; report success rate and average squared acceleration. The text does not specify a train/test split.

datasets.name: Planar pushing (sim-and-target setup from Wei et al. [12])
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the same datasets as Wei et al.: 50 teleoperated target-environment demonstrations and 2,000 motion-planner trajectories from simulation. Evaluate on 200 trials; success means pushing the T to the target pose within the time limit. Report success rate.

datasets.name: Block sorting
datasets.eval_protocol: 50 demonstrations with the correct sorting form the target data; 200 demonstrations with the opposite sorting form the suboptimal data. Report logic as correctly placed blocks divided by placed blocks, motion as placed blocks divided by total blocks, and overall success as correctly placed blocks divided by total blocks. The text reports approximately 800 blocks but does not specify an evaluation trial count or split.

datasets.name: Magic Soup++ (MS++), a subset of Open X-Embodiment (OXE)
datasets.eval_protocol: Used as one of the suboptimal-data mixtures for table cleaning and tower building, alongside task-specific target demonstrations. Evaluate real-world policies on 20 trials per policy. Table cleaning is scored using the task-completion rubric in Table 11; tower building by the number of blocks placed before the tower topples. No train/test split is specified.

datasets.name: Custom OXE (COXE)
datasets.eval_protocol: Used as another suboptimal-data mixture for table cleaning and tower building; it contains MS++ as a subset. Evaluate real-world policies on 20 trials per policy. Table cleaning is scored using the task-completion rubric in Table 11; tower building by the number of blocks placed before the tower topples. No train/test split is specified.

baselines.name: Data filtering
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the target dataset without the suboptimal dataset; compared in the same experimental setups and evaluated with the same task metrics.

baselines.name: Co-training
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared using the same target and suboptimal datasets as Ambient in the controlled experiments; its dataset-mixture weight is swept or tuned in the reported comparisons. In the OXE experiments, both co-training and Ambient use dataset reweighting at each diffusion time.

baselines.name: Finetuning
baselines.fair_comparison: Finetunes the best co-trained policy and the best Ambient policy on the target dataset.

metrics.name: Success rate
metrics.caveat: In the maze and neural motion-planning experiments, success rate measures global task performance but not local motion smoothness; the paper reports average squared acceleration alongside it.

metrics.name: Logic
metrics.caveat: Measures sorting correctness among blocks that were placed, independently of pick-and-place ability; reported alongside motion and overall success rate.

metrics.name: Motion
metrics.caveat: Counts any placed block regardless of whether it went to the correct bin, independently of logical correctness; reported alongside logic and overall success rate.

metrics.name: Overall block-sorting success rate
metrics.caveat: Combines logic and motion as correctly placed blocks divided by total blocks; the paper also reports the two component metrics separately.

metrics.name: Table-cleaning task completion
metrics.caveat: Scored with the task-completion rubric in Table 11; no caveat is stated.

metrics.name: Tower-building height
metrics.caveat: Measured as the number of blocks placed before the tower topples; no caveat is stated.

controls.name: Use only suboptimal data above t_min and target data below t_min in the 2D maze
controls.detail: The policy uses the suboptimal dataset for t in (t_min,T] and the target dataset for t in [0,t_min], rather than using target data at all diffusion times.
controls.rules_out: That the target data must contribute at high noise for the Ambient result; the paper reports performance matching Ambient.

controls.name: Use only suboptimal data below t_max and target data at or above t_max in block sorting
controls.detail: The locality ablation assigns the suboptimal dataset to t in [0,t_max) and the target dataset to t in [t_max,T].
controls.rules_out: That target data must contribute at low noise for the block-sorting result; the paper reports high logic and motion scores.

confounds.name: Block-sorting performance reflects only one of the two skills
confounds.detail: Overall success could appear strong because of sorting logic or pick-and-place ability alone, without demonstrating both.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Report logic (correctly placed blocks divided by placed blocks) and motion (placed blocks divided by total blocks) separately, as well as overall success.

confounds.name: OXE gains are due to dataset reweighting rather than noise-dependent data use
confounds.detail: Reweighting could itself account for the performance advantage over co-training.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Ablate reweighting: Ambient is at most 9% worse without it, while co-trained policies without reweighting are too unsafe to evaluate on hardware; both methods use reweighting in the main comparison.

evidence_standards.name: Evaluation trial counts and reported uncertainty
evidence_standards.detail: The maze and neural motion-planning results use 1,000 trials each, and the planar-pushing results use 200 trials; their tables report asymmetric bounds around the percentages, without specifying the bounds' interpretation in the provided text. OXE results use 20 trials per policy. The paper says OXE finetuning produced no statistically significant change, but does not specify a statistical test or significance threshold.

baselines.name: DP3
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same five tasks, 15 times per policy, with randomized robot starting position, target object placement and instance, and distractors; each task uses at least two types of randomization.

baselines.name: RGB-DP
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same five tasks, 15 times per policy, with randomized robot starting position, target object placement and instance, and distractors; each task uses at least two types of randomization.

baselines.name: ACT
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same five tasks, 15 times per policy, with randomized robot starting position, target object placement and instance, and distractors; each task uses at least two types of randomization.

baselines.name: VR controllers
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared in a 10-participant OmniGibson user study on the same household task; interface exposure was randomized.

baselines.name: Apple Vision Pro
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared in a 10-participant OmniGibson user study on the same household task; interface exposure was randomized.

metrics.name: sub-task success rate
metrics.caveat: High sub-task success can mask compounding errors over long-horizon tasks; the paper also reports end-to-end task success.

metrics.name: replay success rate
metrics.caveat: The paper describes replay success as an indicator of trajectory data quality, not a direct policy-performance measure.

controls.name: WB-VIMA without autoregressive whole-body action decoding
controls.detail: Ablation removes the paper’s autoregressive whole-body action decoding mechanism.
controls.rules_out: A performance gain that does not depend on autoregressive whole-body action decoding.

controls.name: WB-VIMA without multi-modal observation attention
controls.detail: Ablation removes multi-modal observation attention.
controls.rules_out: A performance gain that does not depend on multi-modal observation attention.

controls.name: vanilla diffusion policy
controls.detail: Used as the starting point in the simulation component-addition comparison before adding multi-modal observation attention and autoregressive whole-body action decoding.
controls.rules_out: That the reported improvements require no additions beyond the vanilla diffusion policy.

controls.name: torso or mobile base locked
controls.detail: The paper describes opening-door and dishwasher comparisons with torso or mobile-base movement locked, alongside coordinated whole-body movement.
controls.rules_out: That coordinated torso and base movement is unnecessary for these articulated-object interactions.

confounds.name: Interface-study results could be due to interface exposure order or bias
confounds.detail: Differences in participants’ exposure to the interfaces could otherwise explain differences in success or completion time.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The study randomized interface exposure.

confounds.name: WB-VIMA’s gains could come from explicit 3D perception alone, rather than its whole-body action decoding
confounds.detail: If explicit 3D perception alone explained the gains, the headline performance would not establish the value of autoregressive whole-body action decoding.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper compares WB-VIMA with an ablation without autoregressive whole-body action decoding and reports a further improvement when adding that component to a vanilla diffusion policy.

evidence_standards.name: Real-world policy evaluations: 15 trials per policy
evidence_standards.detail: Trials randomize robot starting position, target object placement and instance, and distractors; each task includes at least two types of randomization. The paper does not specify a statistical test or significance threshold.

evidence_standards.name: Simulation ablation: five runs, 100 rollouts per run
evidence_standards.detail: Results are averaged over the five runs, with error bars showing standard deviation.

evidence_standards.name: Interface user study: 10 participants
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports the participant count and randomized interface exposure; it does not specify a statistical test or significance threshold.

datasets.name: Mimicgen
datasets.eval_protocol: Simulation tasks Stack (951 demos), Stack Three (937), Coffee (768), Kitchen (863), and Mug Cleanup (660). Original Panda/Franka demonstrations were rolled out on the Panda with Robotiq gripper to create the source training data. Policies were evaluated over 100 trials per task and embodiment.

datasets.name: Robomimic
datasets.eval_protocol: Simulation task Can (190 demos). Original Panda/Franka demonstrations were rolled out on the Panda with Robotiq gripper to create the source training data. Policies were evaluated over 100 trials per task and embodiment.

baselines.name: naive baseline (unmodified source training data and unmodified target images)
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses Diffusion Policy; the paper says the same hyperparameters were used for all methods.

baselines.name: Mirage
baselines.fair_comparison: Re-implemented with Diffusion Policy instead of its original LSTM behavior-cloning policy; the same hyperparameters were used for all methods.

baselines.name: source-on-source policy (upper bound)
baselines.fair_comparison: Trained on raw source-robot images and evaluated on the source robot, with no data editing; the paper says the same hyperparameters were used for all methods.

controls.name: black-only ablation
controls.detail: Blacks out the source robot but does not overlay the target-robot mask.
controls.rules_out: If Shadow outperforms this condition, the result cannot be attributed merely to blacking out the source robot; the target-mask overlay contributes to transfer.

confounds.name: Transfer improvement comes merely from blacking out the source robot, rather than from the target-mask overlay
confounds.detail: The headline result could appear if removing source-robot pixels alone were sufficient for transfer.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare Shadow with the black-only ablation on the simulation Stack task: black-only achieved 0.02 on UR5e and 0 on IIWA, while Shadow achieved 0.97 on both.

evidence_standards.name: Trial counts and statistical test
evidence_standards.detail: Main simulation comparisons use 100 trials per evaluation and real-world comparisons use 50; the paper marks methods statistically inferior to Shadow using a two-proportion z-test at α=0.05. Appendix evaluations also report 25 trials for real-world calibration-noise tests and 100 simulation/25 real-world trials for the masking comparison.

evidence_standards.name: Reported diffusion inference settings
evidence_standards.detail: Simulation results use DDPM with 100 inference steps; real-world results use DDIM with 10 inference steps. Real-world policies are executed at 2 Hz.

datasets.name: Human-soft-robot co-manipulation study (HSR)
datasets.eval_protocol: 19 participants; each completed 16 sets of eight planar translations in randomized order. Quantitative comparison uses six sets with consistent robot parameters (CMO center as controller reference point and constant arm stiffness), and only tasks shared with Shaw (2024); task completion time, scaled path length, and velocity are analyzed. NASA-TLX was administered after each set; pre- and post-study surveys were also collected.

datasets.name: Shaw (2024) human-human co-manipulation study (HH)
datasets.eval_protocol: The paper compares against the leader-follower configuration, the closest match to its human-leader/robot-follower setup. Quantitative comparisons use only tasks shared with the HSR study and exclude vertical translations, rotations, and HSR-only diagonal tasks. Shaw’s post-study survey responses are also compared; semantic-differential ratings are converted from a 5-point to a 7-point scale in Table 3.

datasets.name: Freeman et al. (2024) human-human co-manipulation study (HH-F)
datasets.eval_protocol: Used for qualitative comparisons of survey responses, including pre- and post-study responses to identical questions; the study involved human pairs carrying a 27 kg stretcher-like object through obstacles. The paper notes that Freeman’s equal-leader structure and full visual access make motion comparisons less direct.

baselines.name: Shaw (2024) human-human leader-follower teams
baselines.fair_comparison: Quantitative comparisons are restricted to tasks common to both studies; the paper selects the leader-follower configuration as the closest match to its human-leader/robot-follower setup.

baselines.name: Freeman et al. (2024) human-human teams
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper compares shared survey questions and treats this as a qualitative comparison; it notes that Freeman’s participants both had full goal and object-state knowledge, unlike the more asymmetric HSR interaction.

metrics.name: Scaled path length
metrics.caveat: Normalized by direct start-to-goal distance, so 1.0 is the shortest possible path; this scaling enables comparison of straight and diagonal tasks. The paper notes that the small overall difference indicates very similar path efficiency.

metrics.name: Velocity magnitude distributions
metrics.caveat: Similar mean velocities near zero do not show the difference in movement behavior; the paper also reports histograms, which show HH participants maintained higher speeds and spent less time stationary.

metrics.name: Partner-perception survey ratings
metrics.caveat: Comparisons across studies have different interaction contexts: the paper says Shaw’s asymmetric leader-follower setup is more representative of HSR than Freeman’s equal-leader setup with full visual access. Shaw’s semantic-differential responses were converted from a 5-point to a 7-point scale for Table 3.

confounds.name: The robot’s maximum-speed limit explains slower HSR task completion
confounds.detail: A speed cap could make the robot slower even if participants and the controller otherwise supported faster motion.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports that participants rarely approached the robot’s 0.5 m/s maximum velocity, concluding that the longer completion times and perceived slower motion cannot be attributed to the speed limit alone.

confounds.name: Longitudinal-versus-lateral performance differences reflect a robot-specific limitation
confounds.detail: Better forward/backward than lateral performance could otherwise be attributed to a weakness specific to the robot system.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper observes the same longitudinal-over-lateral performance pattern in both HH and HSR teams and interprets the directional preference as inherent to human movement patterns.

confounds.name: Cross-study differences in task and information conditions explain apparent partner-performance differences
confounds.detail: Freeman’s obstacle tasks and equal-leader/full-visibility setup differ from HSR; Shaw’s setup and tasks are closer but not identical.
confounds.ruled_out_by: For quantitative comparison, the paper restricts analysis to tasks shared with Shaw and excludes tasks unique to either study or involving vertical translation or rotation. For survey interpretation, it gives greater weight to Shaw’s asymmetric leader-follower setup and identifies Freeman’s different information structure as a limitation.

evidence_standards.name: 19 human participants
evidence_standards.detail: The HSR study recruited 19 individuals.

evidence_standards.name: Mean and standard deviation
evidence_standards.detail: Quantitative task results are reported as mean ± SD.

evidence_standards.name: Bonferroni-corrected Brunner-Munzel tests with p < 0.05
evidence_standards.detail: The paper uses this test for HH-versus-HSR completion-time comparisons and reports p-values for task-level and overall comparisons; tables mark p-values below 0.05 as significant.
